case_name: In re: Assent, Withholding or Reservation of Bills by the Governor and the President (Presidential Reference, Special Reference No. 1 of 2025)
case_background_and_parties: After the April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor ruling fixed timelines for assent to Bills, the President made an Art. 143 reference (May 2025) asking fourteen questions on whether courts can set timelines or recognise deemed assent. The Union and the States argued the reference.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath, P.S. Narasimha, A.S. Chandurkar
central_legal_question: Can courts fix timelines for Governors and the President to act on State Bills, and can assent be 'deemed' when they do not act?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Limited justiciability of Governor's discretion; no 'deemed assent'; Governor cannot indefinitely sit on Bills
majority_ruling_summary: Advisory opinion: under Art. 200 the Governor may assent, reserve the Bill for the President, or withhold assent and return it with a message; indefinite inaction is not permitted, but courts cannot impose rigid timelines or deem assent, and Art. 142 cannot substitute the Governor's function. Limited judicial direction is possible for prolonged, unexplained delay; merits of the decision are generally not justiciable.
minority_dissenting_view: None; unanimous advisory opinion.
legislative_and_political_impact: Substantially narrowed the April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor ruling; remains central to Centre-State friction with opposition-ruled States.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Core for Federalism, Governor's role, Art. 143 advisory jurisdiction, separation of powers.

case_name: In re: Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 (interim order)
case_background_and_parties: Parliament passed the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 in April 2025. Petitioners including Asaduddin Owaisi, MP Mohammad Jawed and several Muslim organisations challenged it against the Union of India, and sought an interim stay of key provisions.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; CJI B.R. Gavai and Augustine George Masih
central_legal_question: Should key provisions of the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 be stayed pending final adjudication of their validity?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Presumption of constitutionality of statutes; interim stay only in the 'rarest of rare' cases; religious freedom vs state regulation of religious endowments
majority_ruling_summary: Court declined to stay the Act as a whole but stayed specific provisions: the five-year 'practising Muslim' requirement (until rules are framed), the collector's power to decide whether land is government property with effect on waqf status, and capped the number of non-Muslim members on waqf boards.
legislative_and_political_impact: Act continues largely operational; final hearing on constitutional validity pending.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Art. 25-26 and religious endowments; presumption of constitutionality; interim relief standards.

case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu
case_background_and_parties: Governor R.N. Ravi delayed or withheld assent to ten Bills passed by the Tamil Nadu Assembly (many on university vice-chancellor appointments) and returned them. The Assembly re-passed them in November 2023, but the Governor reserved them for the President, so the State of Tamil Nadu filed a writ under Art. 32.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan
central_legal_question: Can a Governor withhold assent to Bills re-passed by the Legislature and reserve them for the President, and what is the time limit for acting?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Governor as constitutional figurehead bound by aid and advice; 'deemed assent' via Art. 142; time-bound constitutional functions
majority_ruling_summary: Held the Governor's reservation of ten re-enacted Bills illegal and deemed them to have assent; laid down timelines (about one to three months) for Governor/President to act, making inaction subject to judicial review.
legislative_and_political_impact: Triggered the President's Art. 143 Reference (May 2025); the Nov 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected deemed assent and rigid timelines.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Governor-State relations, Art. 142, judicial overreach debate; read with the Presidential Reference.

case_name: Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal
case_background_and_parties: The Court's 1967 Azeez Basha ruling denied AMU minority status. Parliament's 1981 amendment to the AMU Act declared it minority-founded, the Allahabad High Court struck that down in 2006, and the Union and AMU appealed; a 2019 bench referred the question to seven judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, Sanjiv Khanna, Surya Kant, J.B. Pardiwala, Dipankar Datta, Manoj Misra, S.C. Sharma (4:3)
central_legal_question: Does a university established by statute lose its minority character, and what is the test for a minority educational institution?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Substance-over-form test for 'established and administered' by a minority; Azeez Basha overruled
majority_ruling_summary: By 4:3, overruled S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India (1967); a statutory origin does not by itself deny minority status; courts must look at who conceived, funded and brought the institution into being. The actual status of AMU was left to a regular bench.
minority_dissenting_view: Justices Surya Kant, Datta and Sharma held AMU, created by an Imperial statute, was not 'established' by the minority and was thus not a minority institution.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reopened AMU's minority-status question; relevant to admission and reservation policies.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Minority educational rights (Art. 30), TMA Pai line of cases.

case_name: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra
case_background_and_parties: Owners of old cessed buildings in Mumbai (Property Owners Association) challenged Chapter VIII-A of the MHADA Act, which let the State acquire such buildings for tenants and was shielded by Art. 31C and Art. 39(b). The challenge against Maharashtra reached a nine-judge reference.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud (8:1 on main issue; Justice Nagarathna partly dissenting, Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia dissenting)
central_legal_question: Are privately owned resources 'material resources of the community' that the State can redistribute under Art. 39(b)?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Limits on State redistribution of private property; economic policy neutrality of the Constitution
majority_ruling_summary: Not every privately owned resource is a material resource of the community; Art. 39(b) may cover some private resources depending on their nature, scarcity, impact on the public and concentration, but the wide 'Marxist' reading in Justice Krishna Iyer's Ranganath Reddy view was rejected.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Dhulia held private resources can fall under Art. 39(b); Justice Nagarathna differed on parts of the reasoning.
legislative_and_political_impact: Settled a long-running debate relevant to MHADA/urban land laws and wealth-redistribution rhetoric.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: DPSP vs fundamental rights; property rights; constitutional economic philosophy.

case_name: In re: Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (Assam Accord)
case_background_and_parties: After the 1985 Assam Accord, Section 6A was inserted in the Citizenship Act to regularise migrants who entered Assam between 1966 and 1971. Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha and other groups challenged it, alleging demographic change and discrimination against Assam.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, Surya Kant, M.M. Sundresh, J.B. Pardiwala, Manoj Misra (4:1)
central_legal_question: Is Section 6A, granting citizenship to Bangladeshi migrants who entered Assam between 1966 and 24 March 1971, constitutionally valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Parliament's competence over citizenship; Assam-specific burden of migration; Art. 29(1) cultural-rights challenge rejected
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld Section 6A; 25 March 1971 cut-off held reasonable as the date of the Bangladesh Liberation War; Art. 355 not violated.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Pardiwala held Section 6A had become unconstitutional with passage of time and unchecked migration, and was open to misuse.
legislative_and_political_impact: Validated the Assam Accord framework; interplay with NRC and CAA 2019.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Citizenship law, NRC/CAA debates, internal security and federalism in the North-East.

case_name: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (SC/ST sub-classification)
case_background_and_parties: Punjab's 2006 Act reserved half of the SC quota for Valmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs. The Punjab and Haryana High Court struck it down following E.V. Chinnaiah (2005), so the State of Punjab appealed (the respondent was Davinder Singh), leading to a seven-judge bench.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, B.R. Gavai, Vikram Nath, Bela M. Trivedi, Pankaj Mithal, Manoj Misra, Satish Chandra Sharma (6:1)
central_legal_question: Can States sub-classify Scheduled Castes for preferential reservation within the SC list?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Substantive equality; permissible sub-classification backed by quantifiable data; E.V. Chinnaiah overruled
majority_ruling_summary: By 6:1, SCs and STs are not a homogeneous class; States may sub-classify based on empirical data of inadequate representation and relative backwardness, but cannot reserve entire quotas for one sub-group or act on political expediency. Several judges suggested a creamy layer for SC/ST.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Bela Trivedi held that Presidential List under Art. 341 cannot be altered by States and sub-classification violates Art. 341(2).
legislative_and_political_impact: Union Cabinet stated it had no plan for a creamy layer for SC/ST; States such as Punjab, Haryana and Telangana moved on sub-categorisation.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Reservation law, creamy layer debate, State powers; follow-up to Indra Sawhney and Jarnail Singh.

case_name: Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India
case_background_and_parties: Mineral-bearing States such as Jharkhand and Odisha levied cess and taxes on mineral rights, but India Cement (1990) had treated royalty as a tax that States could not levy. PSUs including Steel Authority of India challenged the levies, and the conflict between precedents went to nine judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud (8:1); Justice B.V. Nagarathna dissenting
constitutional_articles_involved: Articles 246, 265, 245; Entry 54 List I; Entry 50 List II
central_legal_question: Is royalty on minerals a tax, and can States levy taxes on mineral rights beyond royalty?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Fiscal federalism; royalty is a contractual payment, not tax; States' competence under Entry 50 List II
majority_ruling_summary: Royalty paid under the MMDR Act is not a tax; Parliament's mineral law does not exhaust States' power to tax mineral rights (Entry 50, List II), though Parliament may place limits; India Cement (1990) overruled on royalty-as-tax.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Nagarathna held States cannot tax mineral rights because Parliament's MMDR Act occupies the field and Entry 50 is limited.
legislative_and_political_impact: Mineral-rich States (Odisha, Jharkhand) gained fiscal room; ruling given prospective effect later (from 1 April 2005, payable in instalments).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Centre-State fiscal relations; Seventh Schedule interpretation.

case_name: Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana
case_background_and_parties: Mohd. Abdul Samad, divorced by triple talaq in Telangana, challenged a Family Court order directing him to pay interim maintenance to his former wife under Section 125 CrPC. He argued the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 governed the matter; the High Court had only reduced the amount.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; B.V. Nagarathna and Augustine George Masih
central_legal_question: Can a divorced Muslim woman seek maintenance under Section 125 CrPC despite the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Secular maintenance as a social-justice measure; Shah Bano and Danial Latifi reaffirmed
majority_ruling_summary: Section 125 CrPC applies to all married women irrespective of religion; the 1986 Act does not override it, and a Muslim woman may choose either remedy.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reignited the Shah Bano debate; Uniform Civil Code discussions.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Gender justice, personal law reform, Art. 44.

case_name: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (Great Indian Bustard)
case_background_and_parties: Wildlife conservationist M.K. Ranjitsinh petitioned for the Great Indian Bustard, critically endangered and dying from collisions with power lines in Rajasthan and Gujarat. A 2021 order for undergrounding of lines was challenged by the Union and the renewable-energy sector as impractical.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, J.B. Pardiwala, Manoj Misra
central_legal_question: Is there a constitutional right against the adverse effects of climate change, and can overhead power lines be restricted to protect an endangered species?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Arts. 14 and 21
majority_ruling_summary: Recognised a distinct right against climate change impacts under Arts. 14 and 21; modified earlier blanket undergrounding order and set up an expert committee to balance conservation with renewable energy goals.
legislative_and_political_impact: Shaped renewable-energy siting policy in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Climate jurisprudence, environmental rights, sustainable development.

case_name: Sita Soren v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Sita Soren, a Jharkhand MLA, was accused of taking a bribe to vote for a particular candidate in the 2012 Rajya Sabha election. She claimed immunity under Art. 194(2) relying on P.V. Narasimha Rao; the High Court refused to quash the CBI case and she appealed, leading to a seven-judge reference.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Do MPs/MLAs enjoy parliamentary privilege from prosecution for taking a bribe to vote or speak in the House?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Probity in public life; privilege is not a licence for corruption
majority_ruling_summary: Overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998); bribery is complete on taking the bribe and is not protected by Arts. 105(2)/194(2), irrespective of whether the vote is cast.
legislative_and_political_impact: Strengthens Prevention of Corruption Act application to legislators; relevant to Rajya Sabha poll bribery cases.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Parliamentary privileges, ethics and integrity in public life.

case_name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds Scheme)
case_background_and_parties: The Electoral Bond Scheme was introduced in 2017-18 through the Finance Act and allowed anonymous donations to parties. ADR, CPI(M), Common Cause and others challenged it against the Union of India, saying it hid political funding from voters.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, Sanjiv Khanna, B.R. Gavai, J.B. Pardiwala, Manoj Misra
central_legal_question: Does anonymous political funding through electoral bonds violate the voter's right to information?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Voters' right to information on political funding; proportionality; quid pro quo corruption
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme and related amendments to the Representation of the People Act, Companies Act and Income Tax Act; directed SBI to disclose donor details to the ECI.
legislative_and_political_impact: ECI published bond data in March 2024; major political debate on funding transparency.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Electoral reforms, transparency, Art. 19(1)(a).

case_name: Bilkis Yakub Rasool v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: In 2002 Bilkis Bano, then pregnant, was gang-raped during the Gujarat riots and fourteen relatives were killed. Eleven men were convicted in 2008, but Gujarat granted them remission and released them in August 2022; Bilkis, along with activists and MPs, challenged this before the Court.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; B.V. Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan
central_legal_question: Was Gujarat competent to grant remission to the 11 convicts in the Bilkis Bano gang-rape and murder case, and was the order valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Rule of law; 'appropriate government' for remission is where trial occurred; fraud on court vitiates orders
majority_ruling_summary: Quashed remission; held Maharashtra, not Gujarat, was the appropriate government; the earlier order was obtained by suppression of facts; convicts directed to surrender.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reaffirmed limits on executive clemency in heinous crimes.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Remission powers, Art. 14 arbitrariness, women's safety.

case_name: In re: Article 370 of the Constitution
case_background_and_parties: In August 2019 the President issued orders using Art. 370(1) and Parliament passed the J&K Reorganisation Act, ending J&K's special status and creating two Union Territories. Petitioners including Mohd. Akbar Lone, J&K political parties and lawyers challenged this against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, S.K. Kaul, Sanjiv Khanna, B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant (unanimous, three opinions)
central_legal_question: Was the abrogation of Art. 370 and bifurcation of J&K into UTs constitutionally valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Asymmetric federalism; J&K lacked internal sovereignty; President's powers under Art. 370(3)
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the Presidential Orders (C.O. 272 and 273) and abrogation of Art. 370; held Art. 370 was a temporary provision; upheld creation of the Union Territory of Ladakh; directed restoration of statehood 'at the earliest' and elections by 30 Sept 2024.
legislative_and_political_impact: Assembly elections held in J&K in Sept-Oct 2024; statehood demand continues. Justice Kaul recommended a truth and reconciliation commission.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Union-State relations, special status, federalism, Art. 3 and 356.

case_name: Supriyo @ Supriya Chakraborty v. Union of India (same-sex marriage)
case_background_and_parties: Same-sex couples, among them Supriyo Chakraborty and Abhay Dang, sought legal recognition of their marriage after Navtej decriminalised homosexuality in 2018. Their petitions from various High Courts were transferred to the Supreme Court and opposed by the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, S.K. Kaul, S. Ravindra Bhat, Hima Kohli, P.S. Narasimha
central_legal_question: Is there a fundamental right to marry for same-sex couples, and must the Special Marriage Act be read gender-neutrally?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: No fundamental right to marry; legislative domain; non-discrimination of queer persons
majority_ruling_summary: Unanimously held there is no fundamental right to marry and refused to read down the Special Marriage Act; Court recorded the Centre's assurance to form a committee on rights of queer couples. Majority (3:2) denied right to civil union and joint adoption.
minority_dissenting_view: CJI Chandrachud and Justice Kaul favoured recognising civil unions and queer couples' right to adopt.
legislative_and_political_impact: Union formed a committee under the Cabinet Secretary; legislative reform left to Parliament.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: LGBTQ+ rights, judicial restraint, separation of powers.

case_name: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (services case)
case_background_and_parties: The Delhi government and the Centre disputed who controls the bureaucracy. After the 2018 verdict, the Delhi government challenged a 2015 Home Ministry notification placing 'services' with the Lieutenant Governor, which the Delhi High Court had upheld; a 2019 split verdict took the matter to five judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, M.R. Shah, Krishna Murari, Hima Kohli, P.S. Narasimha
central_legal_question: Who controls 'services' (bureaucracy) in Delhi: the elected government or the Union through the Lieutenant Governor?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Triple chain of accountability; collaborative federalism; democratic principle
majority_ruling_summary: Delhi's elected government has legislative and executive control over services except public order, police and land; officers are accountable to the Council of Ministers.
legislative_and_political_impact: Centre promulgated an Ordinance, later the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023, creating the National Capital Civil Service Authority; challenge pending.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Federalism, Delhi's status, democracy and bureaucratic accountability.

case_name: Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra
case_background_and_parties: In June 2022 Eknath Shinde led a revolt in the Shiv Sena. Governor B.S. Koshyari called a floor test, Uddhav Thackeray resigned and Shinde became Chief Minister. Subhash Desai and others from the Thackeray faction challenged the Governor's and the Speaker's actions.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, M.R. Shah, Krishna Murari, Hima Kohli, P.S. Narasimha
central_legal_question: Was the Governor justified in calling a floor test, and could the Speaker/legislature party appoint the whip after a party split?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Political party, not legislature party, appoints the whip; limits on Governor's use of discretion; split is not a defence under the Tenth Schedule
majority_ruling_summary: Governor's call for floor test was unwarranted; appointment of whip by Speaker was illegal; but status quo ante could not be restored as Uddhav Thackeray had resigned without facing the test. Nabam Rebia reference to a 7-judge bench.
legislative_and_political_impact: Eknath Shinde government continued; later Speaker decisions on disqualification upheld by Court processes.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Anti-defection law, Governor's role, Speaker's powers.

case_name: Madhyamam Broadcasting Ltd. v. Union of India (MediaOne ban)
case_background_and_parties: The Information and Broadcasting Ministry refused to renew the uplink licence of MediaOne, a Malayalam channel run by Madhyamam Broadcasting, citing an adverse Home Ministry security clearance from sealed-cover material. The Kerala High Court upheld the ban, so the company went to the Supreme Court.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; CJI D.Y. Chandrachud and Hima Kohli
central_legal_question: Can the Government deny licence renewal for national security reasons based on sealed-cover material not disclosed to the affected party?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Proportionality; fair procedure; limits on 'sealed cover' jurisprudence; press freedom
majority_ruling_summary: Set aside the ban; held that national security cannot be invoked as a bald claim; non-disclosure of reasons must satisfy proportionality; sealed cover procedure must be balanced by 'public interest immunity' safeguards.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reinforced press freedom against executive claims of national security.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Freedom of press, natural justice, national security and fundamental rights.

case_name: Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (appointment of Election Commissioners)
case_background_and_parties: PILs by Anoop Baranwal and others argued that executive appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners undermined the Election Commission's independence, as Parliament had never made the law contemplated by Art. 324(2). The Union of India was the respondent.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; K.M. Joseph, Ajay Rastogi, Aniruddha Bose, Hrishikesh Roy, C.T. Ravikumar (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Should the appointment of the CEC and Election Commissioners be insulated from executive control?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Independence of the Election Commission as part of free and fair elections (basic structure)
majority_ruling_summary: Until Parliament enacts a law, the CEC and ECs are to be appointed by a committee of the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and the CJI.
legislative_and_political_impact: Parliament passed the CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, replacing the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister; the challenge to the 2023 Act is pending and a two-judge bench was reported to have split on it.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Electoral integrity, constitutional bodies, judiciary-legislature interface.

case_name: Kaushal Kishore v. State of Uttar Pradesh
case_background_and_parties: In 2016 a mother and daughter were gang-raped near Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh. Minister Azam Khan called it a political conspiracy, so the victim's father Kaushal Kishore petitioned for action and for limits on public functionaries' speech, which led to a Constitution Bench.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; S.A. Nazeer, B.R. Gavai, A.S. Bopanna, V. Ramasubramanian, B.V. Nagarathna
central_legal_question: Can additional restrictions be placed on free speech of public functionaries, and is the State vicariously liable for ministers' statements?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Exhaustiveness of Art. 19(2) restrictions; horizontal application of fundamental rights
majority_ruling_summary: No new restrictions beyond Art. 19(2); Arts. 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; State is not vicariously liable for a minister's personal statements, though if made in official capacity, collective responsibility may apply.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Nagarathna (separately) held hate speech is an assault on equality, and Parliament may legislate on ministers' speech.
legislative_and_political_impact: No new guidelines on public functionaries' speech; hate-speech regulation left to Parliament.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Free speech limits, collective responsibility, horizontality of rights.

case_name: Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India (demonetisation)
case_background_and_parties: On 8 November 2016 the Centre announced demonetisation of Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes. Vivek Narayan Sharma and many other petitioners challenged it against the Union and the RBI as beyond Section 26(2) of the RBI Act.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; S.A. Nazeer, B.R. Gavai, A.S. Bopanna, V. Ramasubramanian, B.V. Nagarathna (4:1)
central_legal_question: Was the 2016 demonetisation notification issued within the Centre's power under Section 26(2) RBI Act and was it proportionate?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Judicial restraint in economic policy; reasonable nexus with objective; delegation within statute
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the notification; 'any series' includes all series of notes; decision-making was consistent with RBI consultation; reasonable nexus with objectives.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Nagarathna held demonetisation of all series required a Parliamentary law, not an executive notification, and was unlawful, though no relief was possible.
legislative_and_political_impact: Closed constitutional challenges to the 2016 move.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Delegated legislation, economic policy review, role of RBI.

case_name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (EWS reservation)
case_background_and_parties: Parliament passed the 103rd Amendment in January 2019, providing 10% reservation for economically weaker sections outside SC/ST/OBC groups. Janhit Abhiyan, Youth for Equality, Tamil Nadu's DMK and others challenged it against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI U.U. Lalit, Dinesh Maheshwari, S. Ravindra Bhat, Bela Trivedi, J.B. Pardiwala (3:2)
central_legal_question: Does the 103rd Amendment granting 10% reservation to economically weaker sections violate the basic structure?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Economic criterion as a valid classification; 50% ceiling is not inviolable
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the 103rd Constitutional Amendment; economic backwardness can be a basis for reservation; exclusion of SC/ST/OBC classes does not violate equality code; 50% ceiling applies to 'Indra Sawhney' reservations, not EWS.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Bhat (with CJI Lalit): exclusion of poor SC/ST/OBC is discriminatory and breaches the basic structure; first time Court allowed exclusion-based classification.
legislative_and_political_impact: 10% EWS quota in central jobs and admissions continues.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Reservation framework, basic structure, equality jurisprudence.

case_name: Aishat Shifa v. State of Karnataka (hijab case)
case_background_and_parties: In early 2022 a government pre-university college in Udupi, Karnataka, barred Muslim girls wearing hijab, and the State's uniform order followed. Aishat Shifa and other students lost in the Karnataka High Court in March 2022 and appealed.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; Hemant Gupta and Sudhanshu Dhulia (split verdict)
central_legal_question: Can a State ban hijab in pre-university colleges through uniform rules, and is hijab an essential religious practice?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Essential religious practices test; reasonable accommodation; girl child education
majority_ruling_summary: Justice Gupta upheld the Government Order and Karnataka HC ruling; Justice Dhulia set aside the ban, holding that wearing hijab is a matter of choice, and that essential religious practice is unnecessary to decide.
minority_dissenting_view: Split verdict; matter referred to the CJI for constitution of a larger bench.
legislative_and_political_impact: Referral pending; public debate on school uniform and religious symbols.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Secularism in India; Art. 25 vs public order; ERP test.

case_name: X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi
case_background_and_parties: A 25-year-old unmarried woman, about 23 weeks pregnant from a consensual relationship, sought termination but the Delhi High Court refused because the MTP Rules covered only certain categories (not unmarried women). She appealed to the Supreme Court.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; D.Y. Chandrachud, A.S. Bopanna, J.B. Pardiwala
central_legal_question: Are unmarried women entitled to abortion between 20 and 24 weeks under the MTP Act, and does marital rape count for the MTP Act?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Reproductive autonomy and bodily integrity; purposive interpretation
majority_ruling_summary: Held that unmarried women are covered under the 2021 amended MTP Act up to 24 weeks, and 'marital rape' is included as rape solely for MTP Act purposes.
legislative_and_political_impact: Expanded access to abortion; renewed marital rape debate (Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Women's rights, reproductive autonomy, medical law.

case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (PMLA)
case_background_and_parties: Over 240 petitions, including by Vijay Madanlal Choudhary and Karti Chidambaram, challenged the PMLA as amended in 2012-19, in particular the ED's powers of arrest and attachment, the non-supply of ECIR, the reverse burden of proof and the twin conditions for bail.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; A.M. Khanwilkar, Dinesh Maheshwari, C.T. Ravikumar
central_legal_question: Are the ED's powers of arrest, attachment, search and the 'twin conditions' for bail under the PMLA constitutionally valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Preventive vs penal statute; reverse burden of proof; ECIR need not be supplied
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld Sections 5, 17, 18, 19, 24, 44, 45, 50 of PMLA as amended; ECIR is an internal document, not an FIR; the Money Bill route for amendments left to a larger bench.
legislative_and_political_impact: Review petitions are being heard by a 3-judge bench headed by CJI Surya Kant (reported August 2026).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Economic offences, ED powers, liberty vs state power.

case_name: S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (sedition, Section 124A IPC)
case_background_and_parties: After sedition cases were filed against journalists, activists and critics, retired Major-General S.G. Vombatkere, the Editors Guild of India and others challenged Section 124A IPC against the Union of India. In May 2022 the Centre told the Court it was reconsidering the law.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI N.V. Ramana, Surya Kant, Hima Kohli
central_legal_question: Should Section 124A IPC (sedition) remain operative in light of Kedar Nath Singh (1962) and changing times?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Proportionality in free speech; chilling effect
majority_ruling_summary: Put Section 124A in abeyance pending the Centre's re-examination; stayed pending trials and barred fresh FIRs.
legislative_and_political_impact: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 dropped sedition but added Section 152 on acts endangering sovereignty and integrity.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Sedition law, free speech, colonial laws repealed.

case_name: Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India (Pegasus)
case_background_and_parties: In July 2021 the Pegasus Project reported that Israeli NSO spyware had allegedly been used to target journalists, politicians, activists and judges in India. Advocate M.L. Sharma, journalists N. Ram and Sashi Kumar, and others petitioned the Court against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI N.V. Ramana, Surya Kant, Hima Kohli
central_legal_question: Did the State use Pegasus spyware on citizens, and can 'national security' be a blanket ground to avoid scrutiny?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Surveillance must be lawful, necessary and proportionate; privacy and press freedom; limited scope of 'national security' defence
majority_ruling_summary: Appointed an expert committee under Justice R.V. Raveendran; held that the State cannot get a free pass by merely invoking national security.
legislative_and_political_impact: Committee found no conclusive proof on 5 of 29 phones; Centre did not cooperate; no new surveillance law.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Privacy, surveillance, DPDP Act, press freedom.

case_name: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister, Maharashtra (Maratha reservation)
case_background_and_parties: Maharashtra's 2018 SEBC Act gave Marathas 16% reservation, which the Bombay High Court reduced to 12-13% but upheld in 2019. Petitioners including Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil challenged it, since total quota exceeded the 50% ceiling set in Indra Sawhney.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; Ashok Bhushan, L. Nageswara Rao, S. Abdul Nazeer, Hemant Gupta, S. Ravindra Bhat
central_legal_question: Is the Maratha quota valid beyond the 50% ceiling, and does the 102nd Amendment divest States of power to identify SEBCs?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: 50% ceiling reaffirmed; extraordinary circumstances not shown
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down the Maratha quota; Indra Sawhney not referred to a larger bench; by 3:2, only the President/Parliament can notify SEBCs under Art. 342A.
minority_dissenting_view: Justices Bhat and Nageswara Rao: States retain the power to identify SEBCs.
legislative_and_political_impact: 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 restored States' power to identify SEBCs.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Reservation ceiling, federalism, caste census debate.

case_name: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma
case_background_and_parties: Daughters claiming coparcenary rights in Hindu joint family property (here Vineeta Sharma against her brother Rakesh Sharma in a Delhi family dispute) faced conflicting Supreme Court rulings in Prakash v. Phulavati (2016) and Danamma (2018) on the 2005 amendment, which led to a three-judge reference.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; Arun Mishra, S. Abdul Nazeer, M.R. Shah
constitutional_articles_involved: Articles 14, 15; Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (Section 6, as amended in 2005)
central_legal_question: Are daughters coparceners by birth irrespective of whether their father was alive on 9 September 2005?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Equality in property; coparcenary right by birth
majority_ruling_summary: Daughters have equal coparcenary rights as sons from birth; the 2005 amendment is retroactive in operation; Prakash v. Phulavati overruled.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reinforced gender equality in Hindu inheritance.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Gender justice, personal law reform.

case_name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (internet shutdown)
case_background_and_parties: After the abrogation of Art. 370 in August 2019, mobile, internet and landline services were shut down in Jammu and Kashmir. Anuradha Bhasin, executive editor of Kashmir Times, and Ghulam Nabi Azad challenged the restrictions as violating press freedom and other rights.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B.R. Gavai
central_legal_question: Can the State impose indefinite internet shutdowns and Section 144 CrPC restrictions in Jammu and Kashmir?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Proportionality test; internet as enabling medium for free speech and trade
majority_ruling_summary: Freedom of speech and trade through the internet is protected under Art. 19; indefinite suspension is impermissible; orders must be published and be subject to judicial review; Review Committee safeguards under Telecom Suspension Rules.
legislative_and_political_impact: Telecom Suspension Rules were amended in 2020; shutdown data later cited by Parliamentary committees.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Digital rights, proportionality, internal security.

case_name: Kantaru Rajeevaru v. Indian Young Lawyers Association (Sabarimala review/reference)
case_background_and_parties: After the 2018 Sabarimala verdict, review petitions by Kantaru Rajeevaru (head of the temple's tantri family), the Nair Service Society and others sought reconsideration. The review plus related questions on religious freedom (including other faiths) were heard by a five-judge bench.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge bench; CJI Ranjan Gogoi, A.M. Khanwilkar, Indu Malhotra (majority); R.F. Nariman and D.Y. Chandrachud dissenting (3:2)
central_legal_question: Should the scope of religious freedom and essential religious practices be referred to a larger bench in the Sabarimala review?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Scope of Arts. 25-26 vis-a-vis public order, morality, health; essential religious practices test
majority_ruling_summary: By 3:2 referred broader questions on religious freedom (Sabarimala, mosque entry for women, Parsi women, FGM) to a larger bench without deciding the review.
minority_dissenting_view: Nariman and Chandrachud: review should be dismissed; no reference was needed since the 2018 verdict was correct.
legislative_and_political_impact: A nine-judge bench headed by CJI Surya Kant reserved judgment in the Sabarimala Reference on 14 May 2026 (reported).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Secularism, women's entry to places of worship, religious freedom.

case_name: Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
case_background_and_parties: RTI activist Subhash Chandra Agarwal asked for information about judges' asset declarations and collegium correspondence. The Central Information Commission ordered disclosure, the Delhi High Court agreed in 2010, and the Supreme Court's own Central Public Information Officer appealed.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Ranjan Gogoi, N.V. Ramana, D.Y. Chandrachud, Deepak Gupta, Sanjiv Khanna
central_legal_question: Does the Office of the CJI fall under the RTI Act, and how to balance transparency with privacy and judicial independence?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Proportionality between privacy and transparency; judicial independence is not opacity
majority_ruling_summary: CJI's office is a public authority under RTI Act; collegium decisions' reasons may be disclosed, but not details of candidates' assessments; privacy and fiduciary exemptions subject to public-interest test.
legislative_and_political_impact: Strengthened RTI; RTI amended in 2019 and curtailed by DPDP Act 2023 (Section 44(3)) amendments to Section 8(1)(j).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Transparency, judicial accountability, privacy vs RTI.

case_name: M. Siddiq (D) through LRs v. Mahant Suresh Das (Ayodhya)
case_background_and_parties: The Ayodhya dispute over the Babri Masjid site dates back to the 19th century; idols were placed in 1949 and the mosque was demolished in 1992. The Allahabad High Court in 2010 divided the land three ways; Nirmohi Akhara, the Sunni Waqf Board, Ram Lalla Virajman and heirs of Mohd. Siddiq appealed.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Ranjan Gogoi, S.A. Bobde, D.Y. Chandrachud, Ashok Bhushan, S. Abdul Nazeer (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Who holds title to the disputed land at Ram Janmabhoomi-Babri Masjid, Ayodhya?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Title decided on evidence and preponderance of probabilities; Art. 142 for 'complete justice'; Places of Worship Act as non-retrogression
majority_ruling_summary: Awarded the disputed 2.77 acres to a trust for the Ram temple; directed 5 acres elsewhere in Ayodhya for a mosque; held demolition of 1992 and 1949 placement of idols illegal; ASI findings relied on.
legislative_and_political_impact: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra trust constituted; Places of Worship Act, 1991 debates (Gyanvapi, Mathura).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Secularism, communal harmony, Places of Worship Act, Art. 142.

case_name: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala)
case_background_and_parties: In 2006 the Indian Young Lawyers Association filed a PIL challenging the Sabarimala temple's ban on women aged 10-50, enforced under Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules, 1965. The Kerala High Court had upheld the custom in 1991.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra (4:1)
central_legal_question: Does excluding women aged 10-50 from the Sabarimala temple violate the Constitution?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Constitutional morality; essential religious practices test; 'untouchability' in Art. 17 includes menstruation-based exclusion
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Rule 3(b) of Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules and the exclusion practice; the Ayyappa devotees do not form a separate denomination.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Malhotra: courts should not interfere with deeply held religious beliefs and issues of religious practice unless they are plainly irrational.
legislative_and_political_impact: Mass protests in Kerala; review and larger-bench reference in 2019; nine-judge hearing in 2026.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Religious freedom vs equality, constitutional morality.

case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (adultery)
case_background_and_parties: Joseph Shine, a Kerala-born man living in Italy, challenged Section 497 IPC in 2017 because it punished only the man for adultery while treating the husband as the aggrieved party and the wife as a non-offender.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Is Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC (criminal adultery) constitutional?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Autonomy, dignity and gender equality in marriage; women are not chattel
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Section 497 IPC; adultery remains a ground for divorce but not a crime.
legislative_and_political_impact: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 omitted the adultery offence.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Gender justice, decriminalisation, privacy in intimate relationships.

case_name: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar judgment)
case_background_and_parties: After Aadhaar was made mandatory for welfare benefits, PAN and bank accounts, retired High Court judge K.S. Puttaswamy and others challenged the Aadhaar Act, 2016, passed as a Money Bill, on grounds of privacy and surveillance. The Union of India defended it.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, A.K. Sikri, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Ashok Bhushan (4:1)
central_legal_question: Is the Aadhaar Act, 2016 constitutional, including its passage as a Money Bill and mandatory linking?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Proportionality for privacy intrusion; data protection principles
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld Aadhaar for welfare benefits and PAN-Income Tax linking; struck down Section 57 (private contracting), mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile numbers, and Section 33(2); Money Bill certification upheld.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Chandrachud: Money Bill route was a fraud on the Constitution; Aadhaar Act unconstitutional.
legislative_and_political_impact: Aadhaar and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 allowed voluntary authentication; DPDP Act, 2023.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Privacy, welfare delivery, Money Bill controversy.

case_name: Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (criminalisation of politics)
case_background_and_parties: Public Interest Foundation, an NGO, filed a PIL in 2011 seeking disqualification of people facing serious criminal charges from contesting elections, since many legislators had pending criminal cases. A 2016 order referred the issue to a Constitution Bench.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra
central_legal_question: Can Courts disqualify candidates facing serious criminal charges from contesting elections?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Separation of powers; right to informed vote; limits on judicial law-making
majority_ruling_summary: Court cannot add disqualifications; Parliament urged to legislate; mandated candidates to disclose criminal cases in widely circulated media and parties to publish them.
legislative_and_political_impact: Parliament has not enacted a stricter law; ECI forms revised.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Electoral reforms, judicial restraint.

case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (Section 377)
case_background_and_parties: Dancer Navtej Singh Johar, journalist Sunil Mehra, chef Ritu Dalmia and others petitioned in 2016 because Section 377 IPC criminalised their identities, after the Court's 2013 Koushal verdict reinstated the law. The Union of India left the matter to the Court.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Does Section 377 IPC criminalising consensual same-sex conduct violate fundamental rights?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Transformative constitutionalism; constitutional morality over social morality; sexual orientation as an intrinsic part of identity
majority_ruling_summary: Decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults; Section 377 remains for non-consensual acts and bestiality; Koushal overruled.
legislative_and_political_impact: Led to Supriyo challenge on marriage; the BNS, 2023 omitted Section 377.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: LGBTQ+ rights, dignity, constitutional morality.

case_name: Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra
case_background_and_parties: Dr Subhash Kashinath Mahajan, a Maharashtra pharmacy college officer, was booked under the SC/ST Atrocities Act by a clerk after making adverse remarks in his confidential report. The Bombay High Court refused to quash the case and he appealed, which led the Court to discuss misuse of the Act.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; Adarsh Kumar Goel and U.U. Lalit
central_legal_question: Should arrests under the SC/ST Atrocities Act require preliminary inquiry and prior approval to prevent misuse?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Balancing protection of vulnerable groups with protection against false implication
majority_ruling_summary: Directed preliminary inquiry before FIR and prior approval before arrest of public servants; allowed anticipatory bail.
legislative_and_political_impact: Nationwide protests (Bharat Bandh, April 2018); the SC/ST Amendment Act, 2018 inserted Section 18A to nullify the ruling; upheld in Prathvi Raj Chauhan (2020).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Social justice, legislative override of judgments.

case_name: Common Cause v. Union of India (passive euthanasia and living will)
case_background_and_parties: The NGO Common Cause filed a writ in 2005 seeking recognition of the right to die with dignity and living wills. After Aruna Shanbaug (2011) allowed passive euthanasia with court approval, a 2014 bench referred it to five judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Dipak Misra, A.K. Sikri, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Ashok Bhushan (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Does the right to life include the right to die with dignity, and are advance directives valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to die with dignity; passive euthanasia and advance medical directives
majority_ruling_summary: Recognised passive euthanasia and living wills; laid down guidelines for withdrawing life support; Aruna Shanbaug guidelines modified.
legislative_and_political_impact: Guidelines simplified in 2023; no statute yet on end-of-life care.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Right to die with dignity, medical ethics, Art. 21.

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Right to Privacy)
case_background_and_parties: During the Aadhaar hearings the Union's Attorney General argued that there is no fundamental right to privacy, citing M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962). The petition by K.S. Puttaswamy led to a nine-judge reference in 2017 to decide the question.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; CJI J.S. Khehar, J. Chelameswar, S.A. Bobde, R.K. Agrawal, R.F. Nariman, A.M. Sapre, D.Y. Chandrachud, S.K. Kaul, S. Abdul Nazeer (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Is the right to privacy a fundamental right under the Constitution?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to Privacy; informational self-determination; three-fold test (legality, need, proportionality)
majority_ruling_summary: Privacy is an intrinsic part of Art. 21 and the freedoms in Part III; M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh overruled to the extent inconsistent.
legislative_and_political_impact: Led to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; basis for Navtej, Aadhaar and NALSA-line cases.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Surveillance, data protection, personal liberty.

case_name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (triple talaq)
case_background_and_parties: Shayara Bano of Uttarakhand was divorced in October 2015 by her husband Rizwan Ahmed through instant triple talaq sent in a letter after fifteen years of marriage. She petitioned the Court, supported by Muslim women's groups, against the Union and the Muslim Personal Law Board.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI J.S. Khehar, Kurian Joseph, R.F. Nariman, U.U. Lalit, S. Abdul Nazeer (3:2)
central_legal_question: Is instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) constitutionally valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Manifest arbitrariness as a ground to strike down laws; personal laws subject to fundamental rights (partly)
majority_ruling_summary: Instant triple talaq set aside; Nariman and Lalit held it manifestly arbitrary under Art. 14; Kurian Joseph held it not integral to Islam.
minority_dissenting_view: CJI Khehar and Justice Nazeer: talaq-e-biddat is part of personal law protected by Art. 25 and cannot be struck down; Parliament should legislate.
legislative_and_political_impact: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 criminalised instant triple talaq.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Gender justice, UCC debate, personal law reform.

case_name: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly
case_background_and_parties: In 2015 the Arunachal Pradesh Governor J.P. Rajkhowa advanced the Assembly session, which was held in a community hall, removed Speaker Nabam Rebia and installed Kalikho Pul as Chief Minister after Congress rebellion. Nabam Rebia and others challenged these steps against the Deputy Speaker and the Governor.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; J.S. Khehar, Dipak Misra, M.B. Lokur, P.C. Ghose, N.V. Ramana (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Can the Governor advance the Assembly session and decide its agenda without ministerial advice, and is the Speaker's removal notice a bar to proceedings?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Limited discretion of Governors; Art. 163 interpretation; the Speaker's removal resolution
majority_ruling_summary: The Governor's action advancing the session without aid and advice was unconstitutional; Congress government restored (Nabam Tuki).
legislative_and_political_impact: Led to political churn in Arunachal; the principle was revisited and a 7-judge reference in Subhash Desai (2023).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Governor's powers, Tenth Schedule, federalism.

case_name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (criminal defamation)
case_background_and_parties: Subramanian Swamy, Rahul Gandhi, Arvind Kejriwal and others faced criminal defamation complaints under Sections 499 and 500 IPC. They challenged these provisions against the Union of India as a chilling restriction on free speech.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; Dipak Misra and Prafulla C. Pant
central_legal_question: Is criminal defamation under Sections 499 and 500 IPC an unreasonable restriction on free speech?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Reputation as part of the right to life under Art. 21; balancing of rights
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation, holding reputation is a fundamental right under Art. 21 and restrictions are reasonable.
legislative_and_political_impact: Section 356 BNS retains criminal defamation.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Free speech vs reputation, decriminalisation debate.

case_name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC / Fourth Judges Case)
case_background_and_parties: In 2014 Parliament passed the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act to replace the judges' collegium with a six-member commission including executive representatives. The Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and others challenged it against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; J.S. Khehar, J. Chelameswar, Madan B. Lokur, Kurian Joseph, A.K. Goel (4:1)
central_legal_question: Do the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act, 2014 violate judicial independence and the basic structure?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Independence of the judiciary and separation of powers as basic structure; primacy of judicial voice in appointments
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act; revived the collegium system and invited suggestions to improve it.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Chelameswar: a transparent NJAC does not violate the basic structure; the collegium lacks transparency and accountability.
legislative_and_political_impact: Collegium continues; recurring executive-judiciary friction over appointments and the Memorandum of Procedure.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Judicial appointments, basic structure, executive-judiciary balance.

case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (Section 66A IT Act)
case_background_and_parties: In 2012 two young women in Palghar, Maharashtra, were arrested under Section 66A IT Act over a Facebook post questioning Mumbai's shutdown after Bal Thackeray's death. Law student Shreya Singhal then filed a PIL challenging 66A as vague.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; J. Chelameswar and R.F. Nariman
central_legal_question: Is Section 66A of the IT Act 2000, penalising 'offensive' online messages, constitutional?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Vagueness and overbreadth; chilling effect; distinction between discussion, advocacy and incitement
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Section 66A as vague and violative of Art. 19(1)(a); read down Section 79 and the 2011 Intermediary Rules (takedown only upon court or government order); upheld Section 69A with safeguards.
legislative_and_political_impact: Continued use of 66A by police prompted PUCL's follow-up directions; later IT Rules, 2021 debates.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Online free speech, intermediary liability, digital governance.

case_name: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Transgender activists such as Laxmi Narayan Tripathi and the National Legal Services Authority petitioned for legal recognition of transgender persons as a third gender and for their welfare, after facing discrimination in documents, healthcare, education and jobs.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri
central_legal_question: Should transgender persons be legally recognised as a 'third gender' and entitled to affirmative action?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to self-identified gender; gender identity as part of dignity and personal autonomy
majority_ruling_summary: Recognised transgender persons as a third gender; directed the Centre and States to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for reservations, and to frame welfare schemes.
legislative_and_political_impact: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (criticised for certification requirements).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Gender identity, dignity, inclusive governance.

case_name: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India (NOTA)
case_background_and_parties: PUCL challenged Rules 41(2) and 49-O of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961 because a voter who chose not to vote for any candidate had to say so openly before the presiding officer, violating secrecy of the ballot. The Election Commission and the Union were respondents.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI P. Sathasivam, Ranjana P. Desai, Ranjan Gogoi
central_legal_question: Does the voter have the right to reject all candidates while maintaining secrecy of the vote?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Negative voting as expression; secrecy of the ballot; Rule 49-O struck down
majority_ruling_summary: Directed the ECI to provide a 'None of the Above' option on ballots and EVMs.
legislative_and_political_impact: NOTA introduced in 2013; in Shailesh Manubhai Parmar (2018) the Court held NOTA is not applicable to Rajya Sabha elections.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Electoral reforms, voter choice.

case_name: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Advocate Lily Thomas and the NGO Lok Prahari challenged Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, which let convicted MPs and MLAs continue in office for three months or pending appeal while others were disqualified at once.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; A.K. Patnaik and S.J. Mukhopadhaya
central_legal_question: Can convicted legislators continue in office pending appeal under Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Immediate disqualification on conviction; no special protection to legislators
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Section 8(4); a legislator convicted of an offence with imprisonment of two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction.
legislative_and_political_impact: A 2013 Ordinance to nullify it was withdrawn after public backlash; the rule was applied in later disqualifications of MPs.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Criminalisation of politics, electoral integrity.

case_name: In re: Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 (2G spectrum auction reference)
case_background_and_parties: After the Court cancelled 122 telecom licences in the 2G case (February 2012) and said auction was the proper route for natural resources, the President made an Art. 143 reference asking whether auction is the only constitutionally permissible method for alienating resources.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI S.H. Kapadia
central_legal_question: Must all natural resources be alienated only through auction?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Auction is not a constitutional mandate for all resources; the method must be transparent, fair and aimed at public good (public trust doctrine)
majority_ruling_summary: Auction is one of several permissible methods; for revenue maximisation it is preferred, but policy choices must meet Art. 14 and the public-trust standards. It followed Centre for Public Interest Litigation (2012) that cancelled 122 telecom licences.
legislative_and_political_impact: Spectrum auctions became the norm; coal block cancellation (Manohar Lal Sharma, 2014) followed.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Natural resource governance, public trust doctrine, policy review.

case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
case_background_and_parties: Selvi and other accused persons in criminal investigations were subjected to narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests without proper consent. They challenged these in courts, and appeals from Karnataka and other High Courts were heard together against the State of Karnataka.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; K.G. Balakrishnan, R.V. Raveendran, J.M. Panchal
central_legal_question: Can narco-analysis, polygraph and brain mapping tests be compelled on accused persons?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right against self-incrimination; mental privacy; bodily integrity
majority_ruling_summary: Involuntary administration of these tests violates Arts. 20(3) and 21; voluntary tests are permissible with safeguards and NHRC guidelines.
legislative_and_political_impact: Shaped forensic practices; relevant for Puttaswamy privacy jurisprudence.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Criminal justice reforms, rights of the accused.

case_name: Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (OBC reservation in higher education)
case_background_and_parties: The 93rd Amendment (Art. 15(5)) and the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 gave 27% OBC seats in institutions like IITs, IIMs and AIIMS. Ashoka Kumar Thakur and groups such as Youth for Equality challenged them against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI K.G. Balakrishnan, Arijit Pasayat, C.K. Thakker, R.V. Raveendran, Dalveer Bhandari (4:1)
central_legal_question: Are the 93rd Amendment (Art. 15(5)) and the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 constitutionally valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Creamy layer exclusion applies to OBCs; periodic review of backwardness criteria
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld 27% OBC quota in central institutions excluding the creamy layer; State-aided institutions covered, private unaided not examined.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Bhandari: reservation should be time-bound and caste-based classification needs stricter scrutiny.
legislative_and_political_impact: OBC quota implemented in IITs, IIMs, AIIMS from 2008.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Reservation law, creamy layer, merit vs equity.

case_name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (Ninth Schedule)
case_background_and_parties: I.R. Coelho's estate in Tamil Nadu was taken over under the Gudalur Janmam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1969, which was placed in the Ninth Schedule. His legal heirs challenged the law, and a 1999 reference sent the question of Ninth Schedule immunity to nine judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Y.K. Sabharwal
central_legal_question: Are laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 open to judicial review?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Basic structure test applied to Ninth Schedule; 'rights test' and 'essence of the right' test
majority_ruling_summary: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge for violating fundamental rights that form the basic structure; Art. 31B cannot grant blanket immunity.
legislative_and_political_impact: Curtailed legislative attempts to insulate laws (e.g., 69% TN reservation) from judicial review.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Basic structure, Ninth Schedule, judicial review.

case_name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (reservation in promotions)
case_background_and_parties: M. Nagaraj and others challenged the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments, which restored reservation in promotions and consequential seniority for SC/ST after Indra Sawhney (1992) had barred promotion quotas, as altering the Constitution's basic structure.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Y.K. Sabharwal, K.G. Balakrishnan, S.H. Kapadia, C.K. Thakker, P.K. Balasubramanyan
central_legal_question: Are the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments valid and what conditions apply to SC/ST promotion quotas?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Enabling provisions; quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, overall efficiency; creamy layer applies to SC/ST in promotions
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the amendments but required States to collect quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequate representation and maintain the 50% ceiling.
legislative_and_political_impact: Jarnail Singh (2018) removed the backwardness-data requirement for SC/ST.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Reservation in promotion, Art. 16(4A).

case_name: Prakash Singh v. Union of India (police reforms)
case_background_and_parties: Former Director General of Police Prakash Singh filed a PIL in 1996 seeking implementation of police reforms recommended by the National Police Commission, because political interference in transfers and postings was damaging policing across States.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI Y.K. Sabharwal, C.K. Thakker, P.P. Naolekar
central_legal_question: Should the Court issue binding directions to insulate the police from political interference?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Judicial law-making to fill legislative vacuum; rule of law in policing
majority_ruling_summary: Seven directions: State Security Commissions, DGP selection and two-year tenure, fixed tenure for operational officers, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Establishment Board, Police Complaints Authority, National Security Commission.
legislative_and_political_impact: Patchy State compliance; some States passed Police Acts.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Police reform, governance, federalism.

case_name: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
case_background_and_parties: After T.M.A. Pai (2002) and the Islamic Academy case (2003), private unaided professional colleges in Maharashtra and other States challenged State rules imposing quotas and common entrance tests. P.A. Inamdar and others brought the dispute against the State of Maharashtra to seven judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI R.C. Lahoti
central_legal_question: Can the State impose reservations or its own admission policy on private unaided professional institutions?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Autonomy of private unaided institutions; no State quota; permissible regulation to prevent profiteering
majority_ruling_summary: State cannot impose reservation or take over seat allocation in unaided minority and non-minority professional colleges; regulation allowed for merit and fee.
legislative_and_political_impact: 93rd Constitutional Amendment (Art. 15(5), 2005) enabled reservations in private unaided institutions (except minority).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Education law, minority rights, legislative override.

case_name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
case_background_and_parties: Private educational institutions, including the T.M.A. Pai Foundation in Karnataka, challenged State regulation of fees, admissions and quotas after Unni Krishnan (1993). Conflicting rulings on minority and private institutions' rights led to an eleven-judge bench.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 11-judge Constitution Bench; CJI B.N. Kirpal
central_legal_question: What is the scope of the right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions, and the extent of State regulation of private institutions?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Minority status determined State-wise; autonomy of unaided institutions; ban on capitation fees
majority_ruling_summary: Religious and linguistic minorities are determined with reference to the State; unaided private institutions enjoy autonomy in admissions and fee structures subject to regulation; no capitation fee or profiteering; Unni Krishnan scheme overruled.
legislative_and_political_impact: Followed by Islamic Academy (2003) and P.A. Inamdar (2005).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Education policy, minority rights, Art. 30.

case_name: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms
case_background_and_parties: The Association for Democratic Reforms, formed by IIM Ahmedabad professors, filed a PIL in 1999 seeking disclosure of candidates' criminal records and assets. The Delhi High Court directed the Election Commission to ask for it, and the Union of India appealed.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; M.B. Shah, B.P. Singh, H.K. Sema
central_legal_question: Do voters have a right to know the background of candidates contesting elections?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Voter's right to information as part of Art. 19(1)(a)
majority_ruling_summary: Directed the ECI to require candidates to disclose criminal antecedents, assets and liabilities, and educational qualifications by affidavit.
legislative_and_political_impact: Parliament's attempt to dilute the order via the Representation of the People (Third Amendment) Act, 2002 was struck down in PUCL (2003).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Electoral reforms, transparency, voter awareness.

case_name: In re: Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case)
case_background_and_parties: After confusion over how the 1993 Second Judges Case should operate, President K.R. Narayanan made an Art. 143 reference in 1998 asking nine questions about the meaning of 'consultation' with the Chief Justice in judicial appointments and transfers.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge bench; CJI S.P. Bharucha (advisory opinion)
central_legal_question: What does 'consultation' with the CJI mean in appointments and transfers of judges?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Collegium system expanded; primacy of CJI's collective opinion
majority_ruling_summary: The collegium for the Supreme Court comprises the CJI and four senior-most judges; for High Courts, the CJI and two senior-most judges; the CJI's individual opinion without consultation is not binding on the Government.
legislative_and_political_impact: Basis of the Memorandum of Procedure; the NJAC attempt in 2014 was struck down in 2015.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Judicial appointments, collegium debate.

case_name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
case_background_and_parties: Bhanwari Devi, a government social worker in Rajasthan, was gang-raped in 1992 by upper-caste men after trying to stop a child marriage. Women's groups and NGOs, led by Vishaka, filed a PIL for safe workplaces, as no law on workplace sexual harassment existed.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; CJI J.S. Verma, Sujata V. Manohar, B.N. Kirpal
central_legal_question: How should sexual harassment at the workplace be addressed in the absence of legislation?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Judicial law-making to fill legislative vacuum; use of international conventions (CEDAW) to interpret fundamental rights
majority_ruling_summary: Laid down binding Vishaka Guidelines for preventing and redressing workplace sexual harassment, including a complaints committee.
legislative_and_political_impact: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Women's rights, gender justice, international law in domestic courts.

case_name: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Provisions in Arts. 323A and 323B and the Administrative Tribunals Act barred High Court review of tribunal decisions, a point decided in Sampath Kumar (1987). L. Chandra Kumar and other petitioners challenged these clauses, and the matter went to seven judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI A.M. Ahmadi
central_legal_question: Can Parliament exclude the High Courts' and Supreme Court's judicial review powers over tribunals?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Judicial review as basic structure
majority_ruling_summary: Clauses excluding jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court were unconstitutional; tribunals' decisions are subject to High Court scrutiny before a Division Bench; Sampath Kumar overruled.
legislative_and_political_impact: Shaped the later Tribunals Reforms Act and Rojer Mathew litigation.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Tribunals, basic structure, judicial review.

case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
case_background_and_parties: D.K. Basu, executive chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, wrote to the Chief Justice in 1986 about newspaper reports of deaths in police custody. The letter was treated as a PIL against the State of West Bengal and combined with a similar matter (Ashok Johri) from Uttar Pradesh.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 2-judge bench; Kuldip Singh and A.S. Anand
central_legal_question: How to prevent custodial torture and deaths?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right against custodial violence; compensation as public-law remedy
majority_ruling_summary: Laid down eleven binding requirements on arrest and detention (identification, arrest memo, medical examination, informing family, etc.); custodial death attracts compensation.
legislative_and_political_impact: Incorporated in CrPC Sections 41B, 50A, 54 and later in the BNSS.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Police reforms, human rights, accountability.

case_name: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum filed a PIL in 1991 against the discharge of untreated effluent by tanneries in Tamil Nadu, which polluted the Palar river and the drinking water and farmland of Vellore district.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 3-judge bench; Kuldip Singh, Faizan Uddin, K. Venkataswami
central_legal_question: Can tanneries be allowed to pollute water bodies?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Precautionary principle; polluter pays principle; sustainable development as customary international law
majority_ruling_summary: Recognised the precautionary and polluter-pays principles as part of Indian environmental law; ordered compensation and restoration.
legislative_and_political_impact: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 expressly incorporated them.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Environmental governance, NGT.

case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Karnataka's Chief Minister S.R. Bommai was dismissed in April 1989 under Art. 356 by the Governor after defections, without a floor test. After similar dismissals in other States, including those following the 1992 Babri demolition, all were heard together against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; Justices Sawant, Kuldip Singh, Ahmadi, Jeevan Reddy, Agrawal, Pandian, Verma, Yogeshwar Dayal, Ramaswamy
central_legal_question: Is the President's proclamation under Art. 356 justiciable and when can State governments be dismissed?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Judicial review of President's Rule; secularism as basic structure; floor test as the arbiter of majority
majority_ruling_summary: Proclamation under Art. 356 is subject to judicial review for malafides; Court can restore dismissed government; majority must be tested on the floor of the House.
legislative_and_political_impact: Sharp decline in arbitrary use of Art. 356; Sarkaria/Punchhi Commission reforms.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Federalism, secularism, Governor's role.

case_name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Second Judges Case)
case_background_and_parties: Lawyers' associations and the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association challenged the executive's role in judicial appointments and transfers after S.P. Gupta (1981); the 1990 Subhash Sharma case referred the issue to nine judges.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench; Justice J.S. Verma (7:2); Ahmadi and Punchhi dissenting
central_legal_question: Who has primacy in the appointment and transfer of judges?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Primacy of the CJI's opinion; birth of the collegium; independence of the judiciary
majority_ruling_summary: Overruled S.P. Gupta; the CJI's opinion, formed in consultation with two senior-most judges, has primacy in appointments.
minority_dissenting_view: Ahmadi and Punchhi: executive and judiciary share responsibility in appointments.
legislative_and_political_impact: Collegium system in force; later NJAC struck down (2015).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Judicial appointments and independence.

case_name: Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
case_background_and_parties: Students and private medical and engineering colleges in Andhra Pradesh disputed capitation fees and admission rules for professional courses. Unni Krishnan and others challenged these in the Supreme Court against the State of Andhra Pradesh.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; B.P. Jeevan Reddy
central_legal_question: Is education a fundamental right and can capitation fee be charged by private colleges?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to education up to 14 years as part of Art. 21; capitation fee unconstitutional
