majority_ruling_summary: Citizens have a fundamental right to education up to age 14; beyond that subject to the State's economic capacity; capitation fees invalid; scheme for fee-regulation.
legislative_and_political_impact: 86th Amendment (Art. 21A, 2002); Right to Education Act, 2009; scheme overruled in T.M.A. Pai.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Right to education, DPSP-fundamental rights interplay.

case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission case)
case_background_and_parties: After the Mandal Commission report (1980), Prime Minister V.P. Singh announced 27% OBC reservation in central jobs in August 1990, causing nationwide protests. In 1991 the Narasimha Rao government added 10% for economically backward upper castes, and Indra Sawhney and others challenged both orders against the Union.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 9-judge Constitution Bench (6:3); M.H. Kania CJI, M.N. Venkatachaliah, Ahmadi, Sawant, Thommen, Kuldip Singh, R.M. Sahai, Jeevan Reddy, P.B. Sawant
central_legal_question: Are 27% reservation for OBCs and 10% for economically backward sections in government jobs valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Creamy layer; 50% ceiling; no reservation in promotions; caste as a basis for backwardness
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld 27% OBC quota with the creamy layer excluded; struck down 10% EWS quota of 1991; set 50% ceiling; reservation only in initial appointments; permanent commission for backward classes.
minority_dissenting_view: Justices Thommen, Kuldip Singh and R.M. Sahai disagreed on aspects such as the creamy layer and the scope of Art. 16(4).
legislative_and_political_impact: 77th Amendment (Art. 16(4A), 1995) restored promotion reservation for SC/ST; National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Foundation of reservation jurisprudence.

case_name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu
case_background_and_parties: Kihoto Hollohan, a Nagaland legislator, was disqualified by Speaker Zachillhu under the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law). He and others challenged the 52nd Amendment and the Speaker's final say on disqualification.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench (3:2); M.N. Venkatachaliah; Verma and L.M. Sharma dissenting in part
central_legal_question: Is the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) constitutional and is the Speaker's decision final?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Speaker as tribunal subject to judicial review; anti-defection law consistent with free speech and democracy
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the Tenth Schedule; struck down Paragraph 7 (bar on court jurisdiction) for lack of ratification by States; Speaker's decisions reviewable on limited grounds.
legislative_and_political_impact: 91st Amendment (2003) removed the one-third split exception.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Anti-defection law, Speaker's role.

case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case)
case_background_and_parties: In December 1985 oleum gas leaked from a unit of Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Industries in Delhi, killing one person and affecting many. Environmental lawyer M.C. Mehta filed a PIL against the Union of India and Delhi Administration seeking closure of hazardous units and compensation.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge bench; CJI P.N. Bhagwati, Ranganath Misra, G.L. Oza, M.M. Dutt, K.N. Singh
central_legal_question: What is the liability of hazardous industries for harm caused by accidents?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Absolute liability; 'deep pocket' compensation; no exceptions of Rylands v. Fletcher
majority_ruling_summary: Industries engaged in hazardous activities are absolutely liable to compensate victims; compensation proportional to the enterprise's capacity.
legislative_and_political_impact: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Environmental and industrial liability, PIL.

case_name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
case_background_and_parties: In 1981 Maharashtra's Chief Minister announced the eviction of Bombay's pavement and slum dwellers, who lived near their workplaces. Journalist Olga Tellis and the pavement dwellers petitioned against the Bombay Municipal Corporation, claiming right to livelihood.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Y.V. Chandrachud, Fazal Ali, V.D. Tulzapurkar, O. Chinnappa Reddy, S. Mukharji
central_legal_question: Can the State evict pavement dwellers without notice and alternative accommodation?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Right to livelihood as part of the right to life; DPSPs as aids to interpretation of Art. 21
majority_ruling_summary: Right to livelihood is part of Art. 21; eviction must follow a just, fair and reasonable procedure; no right to encroach on public land.
legislative_and_political_impact: Influenced the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood) Act, 2014 and urban housing policy.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Urban poverty, livelihood rights, Art. 21.

case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
case_background_and_parties: Shah Bano, 62, of Indore was divorced in 1978 by her lawyer husband Mohd. Ahmed Khan after forty-three years of marriage and was paid only mehr. She sought maintenance of Rs 500 per month under Section 125 CrPC; the Madhya Pradesh High Court enhanced it, and he appealed on the basis of Muslim personal law.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; CJI Y.V. Chandrachud, Rangnath Misra, D.A. Desai, O. Chinnappa Reddy, E.S. Venkataramiah (unanimous)
central_legal_question: Is a divorced Muslim woman entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Secular criminal law prevails over personal law; call for Uniform Civil Code
majority_ruling_summary: Section 125 CrPC applies to Muslim women; mehr is not a substitute for maintenance; urged enactment of a UCC.
legislative_and_political_impact: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 diluted the ruling; read down in Danial Latifi (2001).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: UCC, gender justice, secularism.

case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case)
case_background_and_parties: Lawyers challenged the executive's non-confirmation of additional judges and the transfers of High Court judges, including the 1976 transfer of Justice Sankalchand Sheth during the Emergency. S.P. Gupta and others petitioned against the Union of India, raising the meaning of 'consultation' with the CJI.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge bench; P.N. Bhagwati, V.D. Tulzapurkar, Fazal Ali, D.A. Desai, E.S. Venkataramiah, A.P. Sen, R.S. Pathak
central_legal_question: Does 'consultation' with the CJI in judicial appointments mean concurrence?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Executive primacy in judicial appointments; liberalised locus standi and PIL
majority_ruling_summary: Consultation does not mean concurrence; executive had the final say; the Court recognised PIL standing.
legislative_and_political_impact: Overruled by the Second Judges Case (1993).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Judicial appointments, PIL.

case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Minerva Mills, a textile company in Karnataka, was taken over by the Centre in 1974 under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act. It challenged the takeover and also the 39th and 42nd Amendments that protected such laws and limited judicial review.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench (4:1); CJI Y.V. Chandrachud, P.N. Bhagwati, A.C. Gupta, N.L. Untwalia, P.S. Kailasam
central_legal_question: Are Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which curtailed judicial review and gave DPSP supremacy, valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP as basic structure; limited amending power
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Art. 368(4)-(5) and part of Art. 31C; Parliament cannot enlarge its amending power into absolute power.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Bhagwati dissented, upholding the amendments.
legislative_and_political_impact: Reinforced Kesavananda after the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Basic structure, FR-DPSP balance.

case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
case_background_and_parties: Bachan Singh was convicted of murder in Punjab and sentenced to death. He challenged the constitutional validity of the death penalty under Section 302 IPC and the sentencing procedure in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 against the State of Punjab.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench (4:1); Y.V. Chandrachud, R.S. Sarkaria, A.C. Gupta, N.L. Untwalia, P.N. Bhagwati
central_legal_question: Is the death penalty under Section 302 IPC constitutional?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: 'Rarest of rare' doctrine; mitigating and aggravating circumstances balanced
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the death penalty but confined it to the 'rarest of rare' cases with special reasons recorded.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Bhagwati held the death penalty unconstitutional and arbitrary.
legislative_and_political_impact: Section 354(3) CrPC; Machhi Singh (1983) guidelines; BNSS.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Capital punishment, criminal justice.

case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: In July 1977 the Regional Passport Office impounded journalist Maneka Gandhi's passport 'in public interest' without giving reasons or a hearing. She filed a writ against the Union of India saying the Passport Act's procedure was arbitrary.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge Constitution Bench; CJI M.H. Beg, Y.V. Chandrachud, V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, N.L. Untwalia, S. Murtaza Fazal Ali, P.S. Kailasam
central_legal_question: Can the Passport Act be used to impound a passport without a hearing, and what is 'procedure established by law'?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Golden Triangle of Arts. 14, 19, 21; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable; due process
majority_ruling_summary: Overruled Gopalan's narrow reading; any law depriving life or liberty must satisfy Arts. 14 and 19; right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty.
legislative_and_political_impact: 44th Amendment (1978) strengthened Arts. 20-21 protections during Emergencies.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Foundation of Art. 21 expansion.

case_name: A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (Habeas Corpus case)
case_background_and_parties: After the Emergency was declared in June 1975, the President suspended the right to move courts for Arts. 14, 21 and 22. Persons detained under MISA, including Shivkant Shukla, filed habeas corpus petitions in High Courts, and the ADM of Jabalpur appealed against the favourable rulings.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench (4:1); A.N. Ray CJI, M.H. Beg, Y.V. Chandrachud, P.N. Bhagwati; H.R. Khanna dissenting
central_legal_question: Can a person move the court for habeas corpus during the Emergency when Art. 21 is suspended?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Executive supremacy in emergencies (later discredited)
majority_ruling_summary: During the Emergency, with Art. 21 suspended, no one could seek habeas corpus to challenge detention.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice H.R. Khanna: the State cannot deprive life and liberty without authority of law; rule of law survives the Emergency.
legislative_and_political_impact: 44th Amendment (1978); overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Emergency provisions, civil liberties.

case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
case_background_and_parties: Raj Narain lost the 1971 Rae Bareli Lok Sabha election to Indira Gandhi and filed an election petition. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court found her guilty of corrupt practices and voided her election, and she appealed. Parliament then passed the 39th Amendment to protect her election.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench; A.N. Ray CJI, H.R. Khanna, K.K. Mathew, M.H. Beg, Y.V. Chandrachud
central_legal_question: Can Parliament by the 39th Amendment validate the election of the Prime Minister and bar judicial review?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Free and fair elections, rule of law and separation of powers as basic structure
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Art. 329A(4) and (5) as violating the basic structure while upholding Mrs Gandhi's election under the amended Representation of the People Act.
legislative_and_political_impact: Led to the Emergency and the 42nd Amendment; later repealed Art. 329A in 1978.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Basic structure, electoral democracy.

case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
case_background_and_parties: Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Edneer Mutt in Kasaragod, Kerala, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1969, which restricted the mutt's land holdings. In 1970 he filed a petition under Art. 32 that grew into a challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 13-judge Constitution Bench (7:6); S.M. Sikri CJI; dissent by A.N. Ray, D.G. Palekar, K.K. Mathew, M.H. Beg, S.N. Dwivedi, Y.V. Chandrachud
central_legal_question: What are the limits of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Art. 368?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Basic Structure Doctrine
majority_ruling_summary: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure; Golaknath overruled; first part of Art. 31C upheld, second part struck.
minority_dissenting_view: The dissenting judges held that Parliament's amending power under Art. 368 is plenary and unrestricted.
legislative_and_political_impact: 25th, 29th Amendments upheld in part; later 39th and 42nd Amendments partly struck down.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Foundation of constitutional supremacy.

case_name: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalisation case)
case_background_and_parties: In 1969 Parliament nationalised fourteen major banks. Rustom Cavasjee Cooper, a shareholder and director of the Central Bank of India, challenged the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act against the Union of India, claiming inadequate compensation and violation of property and business rights.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 11-judge Constitution Bench (10:1); J.C. Shah
central_legal_question: Is the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969 valid, and do fundamental rights operate in silos?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Effect test: rights are interrelated; compensation must be an equivalent amount
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down the Act for violating Art. 31 (compensation) and Art. 19(1)(f); rejected Gopalan's compartmentalised view of rights.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice A.N. Ray dissented.
legislative_and_political_impact: 25th Amendment (1971) replaced 'compensation' with 'amount'; Parliament re-nationalised banks in 1980.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Property rights, FR interrelationship.

case_name: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
case_background_and_parties: The Golaknath family in Punjab held over 500 acres and was declared to have surplus land under the Punjab Security and Land Tenures Act, 1953. They challenged the law and the 17th Amendment that had put it in the Ninth Schedule, against the State of Punjab.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 11-judge Constitution Bench (6:5); K. Subba Rao CJI
central_legal_question: Can Parliament amend fundamental rights under Art. 368?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Fundamental rights are transcendental and immutable; doctrine of prospective overruling
majority_ruling_summary: Amendments are 'law' under Art. 13(2); Parliament cannot take away or abridge fundamental rights; applied prospectively.
minority_dissenting_view: Five judges held that amendments are not 'law' under Art. 13(2).
legislative_and_political_impact: 24th Amendment (1971) restored Parliament's power; overruled in Kesavananda.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Amendment power evolution.

case_name: In re: Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves
case_background_and_parties: After the 1958 Nehru-Noon Agreement to transfer part of Berubari Union No. 12 in West Bengal to Pakistan, controversy arose over whether Parliament could do this under Art. 3. President Rajendra Prasad made an Art. 143 reference in 1958.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 8-judge bench (Art. 143 reference); B.P. Sinha CJI
central_legal_question: Can Parliament cede Indian territory to Pakistan under Art. 3, or is a constitutional amendment required?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Preamble is not part of the Constitution (later reversed); Art. 3 limited to internal adjustments
majority_ruling_summary: Art. 3 does not cover cession of territory to a foreign State; the Constitution must be amended under Art. 368; Preamble is not a source of power.
legislative_and_political_impact: 9th Amendment (1960) enabled the transfer; the Preamble ruling was reversed in Kesavananda.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Territorial integrity, Art. 3 vs Art. 368, Preamble.

case_name: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
case_background_and_parties: Zamindars such as Raja Shankari Prasad Singh Deo in Bihar challenged the First Amendment (1951), which added Arts. 31A and 31B to protect land reform laws such as the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, against the Union of India.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 5-judge Constitution Bench (unanimous); Patanjali Sastri CJI
central_legal_question: Can Parliament amend fundamental rights, and is a constitutional amendment 'law' under Art. 13(2)?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Parliament's plenary constituent power
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld the First Amendment (land reforms); 'law' in Art. 13(2) means ordinary legislation, not constitutional amendments.
legislative_and_political_impact: Followed in Sajjan Singh; reversed in Golaknath.
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Amendment power, land reforms.

case_name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
case_background_and_parties: After Madras's Communal Government Order allotted college seats by caste and religion, Smt Champakam Dorairajan, a Brahmin applicant denied a medical seat despite her marks, and another candidate for engineering challenged it in 1950 against the State of Madras.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 7-judge bench; Patanjali Sastri CJI
central_legal_question: Is a communal Government Order allotting seats in medical colleges by caste valid?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Fundamental rights prevail over Directive Principles
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down the Communal G.O. as violating Arts. 15(1) and 29(2); Directive Principles must conform to FRs.
legislative_and_political_impact: First Amendment (1951) inserted Art. 15(4).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Origins of reservation and FR-DPSP relationship.

case_name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
case_background_and_parties: Romesh Thappar's English weekly Cross Roads, printed in Bombay, was banned from entering Madras in March 1950 by a government order under the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949. He filed a direct writ in the Supreme Court under Art. 32.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 6-judge bench; Patanjali Sastri, Fazl Ali, M.C. Mahajan, B.K. Mukherjea, S.R. Das, Kania CJI
central_legal_question: Can a State ban the circulation of a journal under a public-order law?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Freedom of the press includes freedom of circulation; 'public order' not originally a ground in Art. 19(2)
majority_ruling_summary: Struck down Section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act.
legislative_and_political_impact: First Amendment (1951) added 'public order' and 'friendly relations with foreign States' to Art. 19(2).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Press freedom, restrictions under Art. 19(2).

case_name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
case_background_and_parties: A.K. Gopalan, a communist leader, was detained in Madras jail under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. He challenged the detention and the Act as violating Arts. 19, 21 and 22 against the State of Madras.
bench_strength_and_key_judges: 6-judge bench; H.J. Kania CJI; Fazl Ali dissenting
central_legal_question: Is the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 valid, and what does 'procedure established by law' mean?
doctrine_or_principle_evolved: Literal interpretation of 'procedure established by law'; watertight compartments of fundamental rights
majority_ruling_summary: Upheld most of the Preventive Detention Act; 'procedure established by law' means procedure enacted by the Legislature, with no due process review.
minority_dissenting_view: Justice Fazl Ali held that procedure must conform to natural justice (due process).
legislative_and_political_impact: Overruled in Maneka Gandhi (1978).
upsc_relevance_and_contemporary_standing: Preventive detention, due process vs procedure established by law.
